origin_region: Phú Thọ · Tân Sơn · Long Cốc
processing: Little is recorded for the commune's green tea beyond what is usual in northern Vietnam: fresh shoots are fixed with heat, rolled and dried. The Bát Tiên variety grown here is also used for oolong-style tea.
harvest_season: Exact picking calendars are not well recorded. As elsewhere in northern Vietnam, tea is picked over a long season from spring into autumn.
appearance_dry: Typically dark green, twisted leaf, as with other northern Vietnamese greens.
appearance_wet: Typically soft, mid-green young leaves and shoots.
taste_profile: Few tasting notes are on record for this tea; expect the fresh, green and gently brisk cup typical of northern Vietnamese green tea.

brewing.notes: General advice for northern Vietnamese green tea; cooler water keeps the bitterness down. Use hotter water if you have the oolong-style lot.

vintage_note: Usually sold as ordinary current-season tea under commune or cooperative labels, without a stated vintage, as is usual for Vietnamese green tea. Drink it within the year. Look for a named cooperative and ask which variety is in the pack, since green and oolong-style products both come from here.
description:
Long Cốc is a commune in Tân Sơn district, Phú Thọ, better known for how it looks than for how its tea has been written about: hundreds of small rounded hills covered in tea bushes, often under morning mist. It is one of the district's largest tea-growing communes.

The variety to know is Bát Tiên, reported as used for oolong-style tea. Visitors also hear about Đinh Bát Tiên and Shan Bát Tiên, offered as the local best. Green tea here is made in the ordinary northern Vietnamese way, as far as anyone has described it.

In the cup, expect what is typical of the region: fresh and green with some briskness. Little has been written about this tea in particular, so brew it gently first and adjust: cooler water, short steeps, then more heat if it seems shy.

Local tea is sold through the commune's cooperative and to visitors, and it also gets promoted as part of the wider Trà Đất Tổ name. A cooperative label with an OCOP star rating tells you who made it, though it says little about the taste.
history:
Little is documented about when tea first went into these hills. Local accounts recall growers having to go elsewhere to obtain tea seed before planting.

The Long Cốc Safe Tea Cooperative was formed in 2018 from an earlier cooperative group. More recently, the hills have become a tourist stop, and provincial authorities have promoted the tea together with tourism.
